news.title: Interior Secretary’s Calendars Dominated by Big Oil and Big Tech, Analysis Finds
news.description: During his first year as head of the U.S. Department of the Interior, Doug Burgum opened his door to a steady stream of corporate executives, trade associations, or their lobbyists, and an outsized proportion of those visitors were representatives of Big Oil and Big Tech, according to a new report released today by Public Citizen. Public Citizen’s analysis of Burgum’s publicly disclosed calendars identified 488 external visitors listed on Burgum’s public schedule and found that more than half, or 262, were corporate executives, trade associations, or their lobbyists. In contrast, Burgum met with 69 visitors from conservation, hunting, fishing, and other nonprofits, accounting for 14% of his visitors, and just 15 visitors from Native tribes. He also had 19 visitors from foreign governments in 2025. “Secretary Burgum’s schedule paints a picture of an official who shows little care for the core mission of the Department of the Interior, while his office becomes a key influence-peddling stop for energy, technology, and finance executives,” said Alan Zibel, a research director with Public Citizen and author of the report. “Burgum’s calendar contains frequent panel discussions, dinners and speaking events with titans of tech, energy and finance but scant focus on our public lands, which have faced mounting attacks.” The Interior Department did not disclose the calendars voluntarily, releasing the 2025 calendars to the public only after a lawsuit by the Sierra Club. The department has not disclosed his calendars for 2026 so far. The analysis of Burgum’s 2025 calendars reveals a clear pattern of promoting corporate interests while deviating from the Interior Department’s core functions, trading the management of national parks and oversight of federal responsibilities to Native American tribes for a flashier profile leading Trump’s National Energy Dominance Council. During his tenure at the Department of the Interior, Burgum has used his time to push the global expansion of oil and gas production, making him a central figure in Trump’s foreign policy misadventures in Iran and Venezuela. His actions promoting Trump’s dangerous energy agenda include citing “national security” to exempt Gulf of Mexico oil and gas drilling from the Endangered Species Act and pushing for offshore drilling off the coast of California, including the use of special wartime authority to force the restart of drilling on a platform that had been idle since 2015 following a disastrous oil spill. Technology has little to do with the Interior Department’s mission, but Burgum has harnessed and bolstered business contacts he made during his former career as a technology executive. Corporate visitors included executives from the largest Big Tech companies, many of which are making huge data center investments, including executives from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Oracle and SpaceX, as well as financial industry titans from Blackstone, Citadel and many others. Additionally, top officials from the United Arab Emirates — Ambassador Yousef Al Otaiba and Sultan Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and CEO of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company — have entries on Burgum’s calendar, as do officials from Canada, Italy and Greece. “As Interior Secretary, Burgum has aggressively worked to redefine the job into a high-profile orchestrator of industry and government,” Zibel said. “But Burgum’s role cheerleading the agenda of America’s CEOs has come at the cost of protecting our public lands, our responsibilities to Native tribes, and investing in low-cost renewable energy. His calendars clearly illustrate how his distracted approach undermines the Interior Department’s goals.” Read the full report here.

news.title: Thanksgiving Prices Jump 11% Under Trump, Gobbling Up More of Families’ Budgets
news.description: Families will pay more for nearly everything on the Thanksgiving table this year, from the turkey to the fixings and holiday pies. A new analysis from Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation finds that the cost of a traditional Thanksgiving dinner is up 11% over the past year, roughly three times the overall rate of inflation, making Thanksgiving yet another expensive holiday for families under President Trump. This year, frozen turkeys – once an affordable option for the Thanksgiving table’s centerpiece – will cost 26% more. Classic Thanksgiving sides will also take a bigger bite out of holiday grocery budgets. Fans of macaroni and cheese will face an astounding 40.2% price hike on elbow macaroni this year. Green bean casserole lovers are in for sticker shock, with green beans up 36.7% and cream of mushroom soup climbing 22.5%. Other holiday favorites have seen price hikes, too, including cornbread mix (9%) and candied yams (10.6%). Dessert offers no sweet relief this year: Pillsbury pie crust is up more than 6%, while Granny Smith apples and pecans have climbed 10%and 23%, respectively. Even wrapping up Thanksgiving leftovers will cost more, with Reynolds Wrap aluminum foil 22.3% more expensive. Higher prices for Thanksgiving staples this year trace back to Trump’s war with Iran and his erratic tariffs. While his war has sent fuel and fertilizer costs soaring, driving up the price of turkey and fresh produce, his tariffs have made traditionally affordable alternatives like canned goods more expensive this year. As prices continue to climb out of reach, recent polling finds that fewer Americans are planning to host Thanksgiving dinner than last year, and many plan to change menu items or cut back on guests. Nearly one-third find hosting this year a financial strain, while almost one in five expect to turn to buy now, pay later loans just to celebrate with loved ones. Groundwork Collaborative Senior Advisor for Economic Policy Emily DiVito shared her reaction: “Thanksiving dinner will cost families more this year thanks to Trump. His war with Iran and reckless tariffs are driving up the cost of nearly everything on the Thanksgiving table, from the turkey to the sides. Working families are in for an expensive holiday season, with less room in their budgets and little patience for a president who promised but failed to bring prices down.” Kyle Moore, Chief Economist at The Century Foundation, said: “Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gathering around the table, but this year many families are deciding how many people they can afford to feed. When the cost of a traditional dinner jumps 11% in a single year and nearly one in five Americans expect to rely on Buy Now, Pay Later loans just to celebrate, it’s a clear sign that household budgets are stretched to their limit. These price hikes are the result of policy choices, and families are footing the bill.”

news.title: At hearing, US Navy chief blasted over Iran war and its toll on sailors
news.description: At hearing, US Navy chief blasted over Iran war and its toll on sailors melissa_fernan… Wed, 18 Nov 2026 - 12:40 Democratic lawmakers tore into President Donald Trump's acting head of the Navy on Tuesday, accusing him of being a Trump "yes man" on the Iran war and downplaying its toll on sailors' mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier. The contentious hearing during the waning days of the Republican-led Senate could be a preview of what's to come when Democrats take control in January after victories in midterm elections earlier this month. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who is seeking to win Senate confirmation to keep the job, did not directly respond to some of the toughest questions before the Senate Armed Services Committee about the Iran war. Those included the cost of the US naval blockade on Iran and the damage to the Navy's headquarters in the Middle East after attacks by Iran. But it was his defense of Navy conditions on board the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group and his praise for the Navy's mental health crisis response that drew the fiercest criticism from Democratic senators. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, asked him about a sailor who went overboard. "Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself and he admitted that," Cao told her, saying he used a life preserver. Gillibrand responded: "What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?" "I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members," Gillibrand replied, adding she thought Cao's response was "inhumane" and "inadequate." Republican Representative Rob Wittman from Virginia extolled Cao as he introduced him as "a remarkable American story," a refugee from Vietnam who served in the Navy for 25 years, including in Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia, retiring at the rank of captain. Cao, whose son is in the Marine Corps, told the committee he wanted the job to ensure sailors "don't go to war the way we did" in Iraq, without armored vehicles or enough body armor. Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, said he was moved by Cao's personal story but said it was also ironic as Trump's administration cuts refugee admissions. "Today, your family wouldn't be let in the country," King said. QUANTITY FOR QUALITY? Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas dismissed talk of poor conditions on Navy ships. "If the picture painted by the Democrats were so bleak, would the Navy have reached its recruiting goals three months early?" he asked. Cao responded, "Senator, we would not be there." Senator Jack Reed, a Democrat from Rhode Island, pointed to data he said showed most new Navy recruits required waivers from standard qualification requirements — including on issues like mental health. "Are you sort of sacrificing quality for quantity?" Reed asked, to a denial from Cao. Cao will himself require a waiver to be confirmed to the job, since he only retired from the Navy in 2021 — putting him below the required seven-year cooling-off period to become its civilian leader. Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published last week found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran once and for all. The Navy has played a critical role in the war, imposing a punishing naval blockade on Iran and helping deliver strikes on Iranian territory. This week, a third aircraft carrier entered Middle East waters, though officials say it is expected to replace one of the two carriers present. While the US military points to the heavy toll imposed on Iran's conventional military, and its ability to help escort tankers through the Strait of Hormuz past Iranian shores, the Pentagon has not yet explained how it sees the conflict ending. Senator Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois, asked whether Cao ever stood up to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war. "Senator, it's not within my purview to do that," Cao said. Duckworth responded sharply: "It is within your purview!" "This is a failure of leadership by President Trump and the unqualified yes-men he's installed, and it sounds like you want to be one of those," she said.
